```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
has_xgboost = requireNamespace("xgboost", quietly = TRUE)
has_purrr   = requireNamespace("purrr", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = has_xgboost)
```

This vignette covers combining models (ensemblers), improving a model automatically (boosters and
random search with templates), comparing many models, and the helper functions for evaluating features,
choosing cut points, handling outliers and clustering.

```{r data, message = FALSE}
library(rml)
set.seed(3)
n = 3000
X = data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n), x3 = runif(n), x4 = rnorm(n), x5 = rnorm(n),
               noise1 = rnorm(n), noise2 = runif(n))
logit = 1.5*X$x1 - X$x2 + 2*(X$x3 > 0.7) + ifelse(X$x4 > 0, X$x5, -X$x5)
y = as.numeric(runif(n) < plogis(logit))
train = sample(n, 2000)
Xtr = X[train, ];  ytr = y[train]
Xte = X[-train, ]; yte = y[-train]
gini = function(model) model$performance(Xte, yte, metrics = 'gini')
```

## Ensemblers

### ENS.RML.AGGR: averaging models

`ENS.RML.AGGR` outputs a row-wise aggregate of its inputs. With classifiers as transformers it averages
their probabilities. It is itself a classifier, so `return`, thresholds and `performance()` work as usual.

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `aggregator` | Name of the function applied to each row (`'mean'`, `'median'`, `'max'`, ...) | `'mean'` |

```{r aggr}
lr  = CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'lr')
xgb = CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'xgb', nrounds = 80, max_depth = 3, eta = 0.1)
avg = ENS.RML.AGGR(name = 'avg', verbose = 0, transformers = list(lr, xgb))
avg$fit(Xtr, ytr)
c(lr = gini(lr), xgb = gini(xgb), average = gini(avg))
```

Fitting the ensemble fitted `lr` and `xgb` too, since transformers are fitted with their parent.

### ENS.RML.BS: a supervisor that picks a model per row

`ENS.RML.BS` combines two classifiers (its pupils). For each training row, the pupil to follow is the
one with the higher probability when `y = 1` and the lower one when `y = 0`. A supervisor classifier
learns that choice from the other inputs; at prediction, the chosen pupil's probability is returned.
Give it the two pupils and a `MAP.RML.IDT` that passes the raw columns to the supervisor.

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pupils` | Names of the two input columns holding the pupils' probabilities | outputs of the classifier transformers |
| `model_class` | Class of the supervisor | `'CLS.XGBOOST'` |
| `model_config` | `list` of arguments of the supervisor | `list()` |

Here one pupil sees only `x1` to `x3` and the other only `x4`, `x5`; the supervisor sees everything:

```{r bs}
bs = ENS.RML.BS(name = 'bs', verbose = 0, model_config = list(nrounds = 50, max_depth = 3),
  transformers = list(
    CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'p1', features.include = c('x1', 'x2', 'x3')),
    CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'p2', nrounds = 50, max_depth = 2, features.include = c('x4', 'x5')),
    MAP.RML.IDT(name = 'raw')))
bs$fit(Xtr, ytr)
c(pupil1 = gini(bs$transformers[[1]]), pupil2 = gini(bs$transformers[[2]]), supervised = gini(bs))
```

### Stacking

Any model can combine others: a logistic regression on the outputs of other models is a stacked
ensemble. Its coefficients are the weights it gives each model.

```{r stack}
stack = CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'stack', verbose = 0, transformers = list(
  CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'm1'),
  CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'm2', nrounds = 80, max_depth = 3, eta = 0.1)))
stack$fit(Xtr, ytr)
gini(stack)
stack$objects$model$coefficients
```

The stacking model here is trained on the same rows its transformers were trained on, which favours
the more overfitted model. Fit the transformers on other data first (a fitted transformer is not refitted)
when this matters.

### Boosting

Gradient transformers, where one model learns to correct another, have their own vignette:
`vignette('rml-gradient-boosting')`.

## Cross-validation

`performance.cv(X, y)` trains a copy of the model on random subsets and scores it on held-out rows. It
returns a list of scores, one per test set. The settings are model arguments:

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `cv.ntrain` | Number of training subsets | 1 |
| `cv.ntest` | Test sets per training subset | 5 |
| `cv.train_ratio` | Share of rows used for training | 0.5 |
| `cv.test_ratio` | Share of the remaining rows in each test set | 0.2 |
| `cv.set` | List of fixed validation sets, `list(list(X = , y = ), ...)`, used instead of random test sets | none |
| `metrics` | Metrics reported (see `correlation()` below) | `'pearson'` for classifiers, `'mae'` for regressors |

```{r cv}
m = CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'cvm', nrounds = 60, max_depth = 3, cv.ntrain = 2, cv.ntest = 3,
                cv.train_ratio = 0.7, metrics = c('gini', 'log_loss'))
scores = m$performance.cv(X, y)
do.call(rbind, lapply(scores, unlist))
```

`evaluate_models(models, X, y)` runs `performance.cv` for each model of a named list and stores the
scores in `model$objects$performance.cv`.

## Comparing models: service_models

`service_models()` fits a list of models, predicts a test set, scores every model and returns the best
one with a results table (one row per model feature, with the model's scores).

```{r service, eval = has_xgboost && has_purrr}
candidates = list(
  CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'logistic'),
  CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'xgb_shallow', nrounds = 100, max_depth = 2, eta = 0.1),
  CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'xgb_deep', nrounds = 100, max_depth = 5, eta = 0.05))
res = service_models(candidates, Xtr, ytr, Xte, yte, metrics = c('gini', 'log_loss'),
                     reported_parameters = c('max_depth'))
res$best_model$name
res$best_performance
unique(res$results[c('model', 'gini', 'log_loss', 'max_depth')])
```

## Boosters

### hp_booster: try values of one hyper-parameter

`hp_booster(base, parameter, values, ...)` makes one copy of `base` per value of `parameter`, then
calls `service_models()` with the remaining arguments.

```{r hp, eval = has_xgboost && has_purrr}
base = CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'xgb', nrounds = 100, eta = 0.1)
hp = hp_booster(base, 'max_depth', c(1, 3, 6), X_train = Xtr, y_train = ytr,
                X_test = Xte, y_test = yte, metrics = 'gini', reported_parameters = 'max_depth')
unique(hp$results[c('model', 'max_depth', 'gini')])
```

### feature_booster: try adding features

`feature_booster(base_model, X, y, n_experiment, subset_size)` builds `n_experiment` copies of the
model, each with `subset_size` extra columns drawn at random from those it does not use yet. It
cross-validates them and returns the best copy if its mean score beats the base model, otherwise
`NULL`. The score is the model's first `metrics` entry.

```{r feature-booster}
small = CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'small', features.include = c('x1', 'noise1'), metrics = 'gini',
                     cv.ntest = 3, verbose = 0)
boosted = feature_booster(small, X, y, n_experiment = 4, subset_size = 2)
if(!is.null(boosted)) boosted$config$features.include
```

## Random model search with templates

`build_model_from_template(template_name, ...)` creates a model with random settings from a named list of
templates. Each template gives the class, sets or random functions for its arguments, and which other
templates may become its transformers and with what probability. The package ships
`default_templates`; you can pass your own list.

```{r templates}
my_templates = list(
  xgb = list(class = 'CLS.XGBOOST', nrounds = c(50, 100), max_depth = 2:5, eta = c(0.05, 0.1),
             transformers = list(list(templates = 'zscore', probability = 0.5))),
  zscore = list(class = 'MAP.RML.ZFS'))
set.seed(10)
search = lapply(1:4, function(i) build_model_from_template('xgb', model_name = paste0('try', i),
                                                           templates = my_templates))
sapply(search, function(m) c(name = m$name, nrounds = m$config$nrounds, max_depth = m$config$max_depth,
                             transformers = length(m$transformers)))
```

`names(default_templates)` lists the shipped templates; `?build_model_from_template` describes the
template fields.

## Feature evaluation

`evaluate_features(X, y, metrics)` scores every column against the target, with summary statistics
when `extra_info = TRUE`:

```{r eval-features}
ef = evaluate_features(X, y, metrics = c('gini', 'pearson'), extra_info = FALSE)
ef[order(-abs(ef$gini)), ]
```

`correlation(x, y, metrics)` is the function behind every `performance()` call. `x` can be a vector or
a table (one score per column). Probability metrics include `gini`, `aurc` (AUC), `log_loss`,
`pearson` and `lift`; with a `threshold` or `quantiles`, classification metrics such as `precision`,
`recall`, `f1`, `accuracy` and `mcc` are available too (see `?correlation` for the full list).

```{r correlation}
p = xgb$predict(Xte)[[1]]
unlist(correlation(p, yte, metrics = c('gini', 'log_loss', 'precision', 'recall', 'f1'), threshold = 0.5))
```

## Choosing a cut point

`optSplit.chi()` and `optSplit.f1()` find the cut point of a score that best separates the classes,
by chi-square association or by F1. `scorer()` gives the confusion counts and rates of a binary
prediction.

```{r splits}
d = data.frame(score = p, label = yte)
unlist(optSplit.chi(d, num_col = 'score', cat_col = 'label'))
unlist(optSplit.f1(d, prob_col = 'score', label_col = 'label'))
d$pred = as.numeric(d$score > 0.5)
unlist(scorer(d, prediction_col = 'pred', actual_col = 'label')[c('tp', 'fp', 'fn', 'tn', 'precision', 'recall', 'f1')])
```

Classifiers use these to set their own threshold: `threshold_determination = 'maximum_f1'` or
`'maximum_chi'` (see `vignette('rml-reference')`).

## Outliers and data checks

`outlier(x, sd_threshold)` flags values more than `sd_threshold` standard deviations from the mean
(optionally repeated on the remaining values with `recursive = TRUE`). `trim_outliers(X)` clips them
in every column; models do this during training with `pp.trim_outliers = TRUE`.

```{r outliers}
v = c(rnorm(200), 15, -12)
which(outlier(v, sd_threshold = 4))
range(trim_outliers(data.frame(v = v))$v)
```

Other helpers: `remove_invariant_features(X)` drops constant columns, `group_features(X)` groups
columns by their number of distinct values, `int_ordinals(X)` turns whole-number columns into
integers, and `na2median(X)` fills missing values with column medians.

## Clustering helpers

`elbow(M, num.clusters)` runs k-means for several numbers of clusters, returns the within-group sum of
squares (`wgss`), the clusterings (`clst`) and a suggested number of clusters (`bnc`, chosen by
`best_num_clusters()`):

```{r elbow}
M = scale(X[c('x1', 'x2', 'x3')])
el = elbow(M, num.clusters = c(2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12), doPlot = FALSE)
round(el$wgss)
el$bnc
```

`cluster_tree(distmat)` runs a hierarchical clustering on a distance matrix and reports the clusters for
each number of clusters. These functions underlie the `BIN.*` clustering transformers described in
`vignette('rml-transformers')`.

## Saving and loading

`model_save(model, path)` writes the model, with its transformers and any Python or keras objects, into
the folder `path/<model name>`. `model_load(name, path)` reads it back.

```{r save}
folder = tempfile()
model_save(avg, folder)
avg2 = model_load('avg', folder)
all.equal(avg$predict(Xte[1:5, ]), avg2$predict(Xte[1:5, ]))
```
